newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian local polls largely free of controversy.
newsitem.headline: Albanian local polls largely free of controversy.

text.p: Albanians turned out in force to vote in local polls largely free of the controversy that marred the Balkan nation's parliamentary elections five months ago.
Western monitors kept a close watch on Sunday's ballot, considered by the United States and the European Union to be a test of the ruling Democratic Party's commitment to democracy.
"In general, the voting process has gone on normally and there were no worrying problems," said Nestor Thereska, chairman of Albania's Central Elections Commission.
The Council of Europe, which coordinated monitoring of the vote, said it was too early to draw final conclusions but added there had been no reports of serious incidents.
"We have to wait for our people to tell us what they have found. I must say none of our observers has called in to report any dramatic occurrences," said a Council of Europe official.
The Central Elections Commission authorised 365 international observers to monitor the vote, according to Albanian news agency ATA.
The Council of Europe said its officials were present at polling stations to oversee the counting. Earlier it praised the level of cooperation it had received.
President Sali Berisha, a heart surgeon turned politician, assured Albanian voters and the international community that the poll would be free and fair as he cast his ballot in the capital Tirana.
Turnout was estimated at around 70 percent by early evening. Most polling stations closed at 9 p.m. (1900 GMT).

Most opposition parties, including the key Socialists, pulled out of general elections in May and June alleging vote rigging by Berisha's Democrats - charges upheld by some internatonal observers. The Democrats claimed a landslide victory in the vote.
On Sunday, the Democratic Party and the Socialists waged a war of faxes, denouncing each other for alleged irregularities, especially in rural areas and smaller towns.
The Socialist Party, reformed heirs to the communists, claimed police had forced their way into voting booths and tampered with ballot boxes. The Interior Ministry swiftly issued a denial.
The Democrats in turn accused Socialist supporters of intimidating voters by surrounding polling stations.

Some 2.2 million Albanians were eligible to take part in the ballot. Most appeared to take the vote in their stride. "Everything was calm and the situation was stable," said Zoi, a retired man living in the capital.
Results of the fight for influence in 64 town councils, 36 district councils and 310 communes are expected early this week.
In the last local polls in July 1992, the Socialists won more town halls than the Democrats but the governing party took all the big cities, including Tirana.
